uncertainty_note: Detailed disclosure subtree not provided in retrieved context; node id chosen by best judgement.

title: Secondary use of uploaded videos beyond moderation
description: The service may use uploaded videos or metadata for purposes not expected by the parent, such as model training, analytics, product improvement, or marketing-related profiling, beyond the immediate approval/rejection purpose.
assumptions: The destination process has technical and organizational ability to retain and repurpose uploaded content.
uncertainty_note: Specific Unawareness subtree id is approximate because the retrieved context did not include detailed U nodes.

title: Improper personal data management of uploaded child videos
description: The Video Management Service may process or retain uploaded videos and associated metadata without adequate minimization, retention limits, lawful basis handling, parental transparency, or child-specific safeguards, creating non-compliance risk.
assumptions: The uploaded content contains personal data, potentially special-category or child-related data subject to stricter obligations.

title: Insufficient evidence of parent consent or submission intent
description: If the service does not capture reliable records of who uploaded the video, what was submitted, and under which consent/notice terms, the parent may later be unable to prove or dispute the submission and the organization may be unable to demonstrate valid authorization for processing.
assumptions: The workflow relies on parental authorization or acceptance of terms for child-related uploads.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation-related subtree id is approximate due to absent detailed threat-tree excerpt.

title: Streaming reveals the child's viewing choice to the service
description: By sending a specific approved video stream to the child, the Video Management Service necessarily processes and discloses information about which content this child is watching at this moment. If this viewing event is unnecessary for the stated purpose, overly granular, or exposed internally beyond need-to-know, it creates a detectability threat because observers or internal parties can detect the child's consumption of particular content.
assumptions: Assumes the stream request/response is associated with a child-specific session or account rather than being fully anonymous broadcast delivery.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate; retrieved context did not include detailed D threat-tree nodes.

title: Video-stream metadata can link repeated sessions to the same child or household
description: Even if the video payload itself is approved content, metadata on the flow such as persistent session identifiers, IP address, device identifiers, CDN tokens, timing patterns, or stable request URLs can allow repeated viewing sessions to be linked to the same child, device, or household.
assumptions: Assumes the streaming flow carries stable identifiers or observable network metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate; retrieved context only confirmed L is applicable for Process→ExternalEntity flows.

title: Streaming flow metadata may identify the child or household
description: Identifiers or quasi-identifiers in the streaming transaction—such as account-linked tokens, IP address, device IDs, or uniquely identifying URLs—may permit identification of the child user or their household by network observers or intermediaries.
assumptions: Assumes the stream is not fully anonymized and that network/intermediary parties can observe metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate; exact I subtree node not provided in retrieved context.

title: Network observers can detect that the child is watching a particular video or service
description: Traffic characteristics of the stream, including destination hostnames, URL paths, content identifiers, bitrate patterns, or timing, may allow an observer to detect that the child is using this video service and possibly infer the specific approved video being watched.
assumptions: Assumes transport/network metadata is visible to some observer, even if payload is encrypted.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate; exact D subtree node not provided in retrieved context.

title: Video content displayed to the child may expose sensitive attributes to nearby observers
description: Once received and rendered at the child's device, the stream can be seen or heard by parents, siblings, peers, or others nearby, making the child's viewing choices or inferred interests detectable in the physical environment.
assumptions: Assumes the child consumes the stream in a setting where shoulder-surfing or overhearing is possible.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate and this is context-dependent.

title: Streaming child-directed content may involve non-compliant personal-data handling
description: Delivering a personalized or session-bound video stream to a child may involve processing children's personal data (e.g., account/session identifiers, viewing history, parental-control state). If the service lacks an appropriate legal basis, age-appropriate transparency, parental authorization where required, or data-minimization controls, this flow can contribute to non-compliance.
assumptions: Assumes the service is subject to child-privacy obligations and the stream is tied to personal data rather than anonymous delivery.

title: Excessive disclosure of child browsing data from the profile store
description: The childprofiles collection may disclose more personal data than is strictly necessary when sending browsing data to the AI Recommendation Engine. Because the data concerns children and browsing behavior, unnecessary attributes, long history, or highly granular events could expose sensitive interests and habits beyond what is needed for recommendation generation.
assumptions: Assumes the AI engine does not require the full raw browsing history or all profile attributes for its intended function.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimization structure; exact subnode may differ in your local taxonomy.

title: AI engine may process child browsing data for purposes users did not expect
description: On receipt of the browsing data, the AI Recommendation Engine may use it for profiling, model improvement, experimentation, or inference beyond the originally understood purpose of providing recommendations. This can create an unawareness threat if children or guardians are not adequately informed about how the data is used.
assumptions: Assumes notices or consent flows may not clearly explain AI-based profiling, secondary use, or model-training-related processing.
uncertainty_note: Exact U subnode is inferred from standard LINDDUN unawareness patterns; confirm against your threat-tree version.

title: AI engine can infer sensitive traits or preferences from browsing data
description: The destination process may derive new personal information from the child's browsing history, such as interests, vulnerabilities, routines, maturity level, or potentially sensitive categories. Even if only browsing events are sent, the AI engine's analysis can increase detectability of intimate attributes about the child.
assumptions: Assumes recommendation models perform behavioral profiling or feature extraction from browsing history.
uncertainty_note: Detectability is grounded in inference/derivation at the destination; exact node id may vary by LINDDUN Pro edition.

title: Browsing data may be linked with other identifiers or datasets in the AI engine
description: Once received by the AI Recommendation Engine, the browsing data may be combined with account, device, session, or model telemetry data, enabling linkage of records across contexts and over time. This can create richer child profiles than intended.
assumptions: Assumes P4 has access to persistent identifiers, telemetry, or other datasets that can be joined with the incoming browsing data.
uncertainty_note: Linkability applies if the AI engine can correlate this flow with other records; validate whether such identifiers are present.

title: Child may become identifiable to the AI engine through direct or indirect identifiers
description: Although the flow is described as browsing data, the received dataset may contain direct identifiers or quasi-identifiers such as profile IDs, device IDs, timestamps, rare browsing patterns, or contextual attributes that allow the AI engine to identify a specific child.
assumptions: Assumes the payload includes identifiers or sufficiently unique behavioral/contextual data.
uncertainty_note: Identifiability depends on the actual schema and uniqueness of the browsing data sent in DF13.

title: Processing child browsing data for AI recommendations may lack a valid legal basis or exceed consent
description: Because this flow involves children's browsing data and AI-driven profiling, the destination processing may be non-compliant if it proceeds without an appropriate legal basis, age-appropriate transparency, parental authorization where required, or adherence to purpose limitation and data minimization obligations.
assumptions: Assumes the system operates in a jurisdiction with heightened protections for children's data and profiling.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations are jurisdiction-specific; confirm applicable law and whether parental consent or another legal basis is relied upon.

title: Unnecessary disclosure of browsing data to third-party advertisers
description: The AI Recommendation Engine plans to share users' browsing data with third-party advertisers. Browsing data is personal data and may reveal interests, habits, and potentially sensitive inferences. Sending it to advertisers constitutes an explicit disclosure across a trust boundary that may be avoidable if not strictly necessary for the recommendation service.
assumptions: Assumes the browsing data relates to identifiable or reasonably linkable users and that sharing with advertisers is not strictly necessary for the core service requested by the user.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement for explicit/avoidable third-party disclosure; exact sub-node naming may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Secondary use of browsing data by advertisers beyond user expectations
description: Once received, third-party advertisers may use the browsing data for profiling, ad targeting, audience enrichment, or other downstream purposes beyond the original context in which the data was collected. This creates an unawareness threat if users are not adequately informed that their browsing behavior will be used by external advertisers.
assumptions: Assumes users may not reasonably expect direct sharing of browsing data with external advertisers and that notices/controls may be insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Applicable as a destination-side unawareness threat, but exact threat-tree sub-node may differ depending on the project's LINDDUN Pro catalog.

title: Sharing browsing data with advertisers may exceed or conflict with user consent
description: If users have not given specific, informed, and freely given consent for disclosure of browsing data to third-party advertisers, or if the sharing exceeds the scope of consent originally obtained, the destination's receipt and processing of the data creates a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes browsing data is subject to consent/transparency requirements and that advertiser sharing is planned rather than already validated against a lawful basis.
uncertainty_note: This depends on the actual legal basis, notices, and consent mechanism in scope; exact node id is best-effort.

title: Advertisers can link browsing data with existing profiles
description: Third-party advertisers commonly possess identifiers, cookies, device fingerprints, or account-level data that can be combined with received browsing data. This enables linking the transferred data to existing user profiles across services or contexts, increasing privacy risk.
assumptions: Assumes advertisers have independent datasets or identifiers enabling correlation with the received browsing data.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node id is best-effort; the applicability of linkability is strong given the recipient type and data category.

title: Browsing data may enable identification by advertisers
description: Even if the shared browsing data is not overtly labeled with a real name, advertisers may identify individuals by combining browsing patterns with persistent identifiers, account data, IP-related information, or other auxiliary datasets. Receipt of the data therefore creates an identifiability threat.
assumptions: Assumes the transferred browsing data includes or is accompanied by identifiers or sufficiently distinctive behavioral patterns.
uncertainty_note: Identification may depend on the exact fields shared; threat remains plausible because advertisers often have strong auxiliary data.

title: Collection and storage of government ID images may exceed data minimization
description: The Authentication Service sends full government ID images to persistent storage. Government ID images are highly sensitive personal data and often contain more attributes than are strictly necessary for authentication or verification. If the service stores complete images where a narrower attribute set, extracted fields, or a one-time verification result would suffice, this flow creates an avoidable data disclosure by design.
assumptions: Assumes the system's purpose can be achieved without retaining full ID images indefinitely, or without storing all image content in raw form.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement for explicit disclosure / excessive collection-storage under Dd; exact sub-node naming may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: ID images may be exposed in transit to backend storage
description: This flow transfers government ID images from the Authentication Service to the file system. If the transfer path, storage API, logging, temporary buffers, or transport protections are insufficient, the images could be disclosed during transmission or via transfer-related metadata and intermediaries. Because the data is highly sensitive, any unnecessary exposure on the path constitutes a significant disclosure threat.
assumptions: Assumes the flow may traverse components, interfaces, or logs where the image content or metadata could be observed beyond strictly necessary recipients.
uncertainty_note: Exact Dd sub-node citation is approximate; threat applicability is strong, but the precise tree-node label may differ.

title: Persistent storage of raw government ID images may enable unnecessary disclosure at rest
description: The File System receives and stores raw government ID images in backend/uploads/. Retaining these images at rest increases the chance of later disclosure to internal parties, administrators, backup systems, or other downstream recipients who do not need full image access. If retention is longer than necessary or access scope is broader than required, the destination's handling creates an avoidable disclosure threat.
assumptions: Assumes stored files may be retained, backed up, or accessed by roles and systems beyond the immediate verification purpose.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is an approximate best-fit for unnecessary storage/retention disclosure at the destination.

title: Storing government ID images may be non-compliant with legal basis, retention, or special handling obligations
description: Government ID images are typically subject to strict legal and regulatory requirements, including lawful basis, purpose limitation, retention limits, access restrictions, and possibly jurisdiction-specific identity-document rules. Writing these images to a general backend file system may violate such obligations if the storage design does not enforce them.
assumptions: Assumes the system operates in a regulated context where identity-document processing is governed by privacy/data-protection law or sector-specific rules.
uncertainty_note: Exact Nc sub-node citation is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the non-compliance tree.

title: Users may be unaware that full government ID images are stored in backend uploads
description: If the system stores uploaded government ID images in backend/uploads/ without clearly informing users about the storage, retention period, purpose, and recipients, data subjects may lack awareness of how their identity documents are processed. This undermines transparency for a particularly sensitive category of personal data.
assumptions: Assumes notices or just-in-time explanations may be absent, incomplete, or not specific about persistent storage of the images.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; applicability depends on whether transparent notice is actually provided.

title: JWT in localStorage enables cross-context linkability
description: Storing a persistent JWT in browser localStorage allows the same browser context to present the same token across sessions and application interactions. Any script with access to the origin's localStorage can reuse the token value to correlate a user's activities over time within that origin, making separate visits or actions linkable.
assumptions: The JWT is long-lived enough to be reused across multiple interactions, and application scripts or embedded third-party scripts can access localStorage for this origin.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include the detailed LINDDUN threat tree.

title: JWT stored client-side can identify the user or account
description: A JWT commonly contains stable identifiers or claims about the authenticated subject. When stored in localStorage, the token can be read by scripts running in the page context and used to identify the user, account, or session associated with the browser.
assumptions: The JWT contains subject, account, role, or other identifying claims, or can be dereferenced server-side to a specific user.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is approximate; applicability is strong because JWTs typically encode or reference identity.

title: JWT contents may disclose personal or sensitive claims
description: If the JWT includes readable claims such as user identifiers, email address, roles, tenant information, or other attributes, storing it in localStorage exposes those claims to any script able to access the storage. This can disclose personal data beyond what is necessary for client-side operation.
assumptions: The JWT is not encrypted as a JWE and contains privacy-relevant claims in plaintext/base64url-encoded form.
uncertainty_note: Whether disclosure occurs depends on the actual JWT payload contents.

title: Users may be unaware that authentication tokens persist in localStorage
description: Persisting a JWT in localStorage can create a hidden, durable authenticated state that survives browser restarts until explicit removal. Users may not expect this persistence or understand that logout, shared-device use, or browser closure may not fully clear the token unless the application removes it.
assumptions: The application does not clearly communicate token persistence and lifecycle to users.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; threat depends on the application's transparency and UX.

title: Storing JWT in localStorage may exceed necessity for client-side authentication
description: Using localStorage for JWT persistence may collect or retain authentication data longer than necessary compared with less persistent or more constrained mechanisms. If the full token is stored client-side without strict retention limits, this can conflict with data minimization and storage limitation expectations.
assumptions: A less privacy-intrusive design is feasible, such as short-lived in-memory tokens or more constrained session handling.
uncertainty_note: Necessity/compliance depends on system requirements and applicable policy or legal basis.

title: Excessive disclosure of child history to parent
description: The process may disclose more of the child's history than is necessary for the parent's review purpose, such as detailed events, timestamps, notes, or historical records beyond the intended scope. This creates a privacy risk because sensitive child-related information is shared externally.
assumptions: Assumes the parent does not always need the full historical record and that some history items may be sensitive or unnecessary for the immediate review task.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement; exact sub-node may vary depending on the project's threat-tree version.

title: Secondary use of child history without adequate purpose limitation
description: The process may provide child history to the parent in a way that enables use beyond the original purpose for which the history was collected, such as broader monitoring, profiling, or reuse outside the expected review context.
assumptions: Assumes some child history was originally collected for operational or safeguarding purposes and not all downstream parental uses are necessarily aligned with that original purpose.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on the stated purposes and governance around parental access.

title: Parent can plausibly deny having received or reviewed child history
description: If receipt or review of the child history is not logged or evidenced, the parent may later deny having accessed the information. This undermines accountability for disclosures of sensitive child data.
assumptions: Assumes the system relies on accountability for sensitive disclosures and does not provide strong evidence of receipt or access.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation in privacy modeling can be context-sensitive; included here because accountability for sensitive disclosures appears relevant.

title: Child identity or profile may be inferred from data in transit or flow metadata
description: The content of the transmitted history, or metadata about the transfer such as account identifiers, child identifiers, timing, and frequency, may allow identification of the child or parent-child relationship by parties observing the flow.
assumptions: Assumes the flow carries identifiers or distinctive quasi-identifiers, or that transport metadata is observable to intermediaries or logs.
uncertainty_note: Exact identification mechanism depends on transport protections and what metadata is exposed.

title: Flow metadata enables linking of child records across interactions
description: Recurring identifiers or stable metadata in repeated history retrievals can allow observers or system components handling the flow to link multiple accesses to the same child or family over time, building a profile of the child's activities or issues.
assumptions: Assumes repeated requests/responses use stable identifiers, session data, or recognizable patterns that can be correlated.
uncertainty_note: Included based on common linkage risks in repeated profile/history retrieval; exact linkage vector is architecture-dependent.

title: Parent may retain or further disclose child history after receipt
description: Once the parent receives the child history, they may store, copy, screenshot, or share it onward beyond the intended audience or retention period. This creates a dissemination risk for sensitive child information outside system control.
assumptions: Assumes the parent interface allows viewing or exporting information and that downstream handling by the parent is not technically constrained.
uncertainty_note: This is a common risk for disclosures to external entities, but exact likelihood depends on interface controls and policy enforcement.

title: Child history may be provided to parent without valid consent, authority, or legal basis
description: The receiving parent may not have appropriate authority to access all parts of the child's history, for example due to custody limitations, age-related confidentiality rules, or missing/withdrawn consent. Delivering the history in such cases creates a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes access rights can vary by parent, child age, jurisdiction, or record category, and that not all history is uniformly shareable.
uncertainty_note: Strongly applicable in many child-data contexts, though exact legal basis depends on jurisdiction and business rules.
